title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 349
paragraphs: This king also left behind him a pyramid, much smaller than his father's, square in shape and measuring three hundred feet lacking twenty on each side, built moreover of Ethiopian stone up to half its height. This pyramid some of the Greeks claim was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, but in saying this they are not speaking correctly. Besides, it is obvious to me that those who say this do not even know who Rhodopis was — otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which, so to speak, countless thousands of talents were spent. Moreover, they do not know that Rhodopis flourished in the reign of Amasis, not in this king's reign, for Rhodopis lived many years later than the kings who left behind the pyramids. By descent she was Thracian, and she was a slave of Iadmon son of Hephaistopolis, a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker — for he too was once the slave of Iadmon, as was proved especially by this fact: when the people of Delphi repeatedly proclaimed, in accordance with an oracle, that someone should claim the blood-money for Aesop's death, no one else came forward, but at length the grandson of Iadmon, also called Iadmon, claimed it; and so it is shown that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.
